title: WEEKEND READING: UUK Contextual Admissions Guidance: A Response

The post WEEKEND READING: UUK Contextual Admissions Guidance: A Response appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Tom Fryer, Charlie Deeks, Sylvie Lomer, Paul Smith and Steven Jones, all of HERE@Manchester, the Higher Education research group based at University of Manchester.

On 10th July 2026, Universities UK (UUK) published Contextual Admission: A guide to fair and transparent practice, which provides guidance on the practice of contextual admissions in English universities, forming an appendix to UUK-GuildHE Fair Admissions Code of Practice. The document was developed in collaboration with UCAS and the Sutton Trust, and aims to guide contextual admissions practices to ensure that they are fair, transparent, and delivered to best support widening participation.

The publication is a welcome intervention. Sector-level discussion on the principles and practice of contextual admissions is essential, both to clarify expectations around good practice, as well as to support the development of a more consistent approach that applicants and their advisors can navigate. We share UUK’s hope that this results in a fairer and more transparent process, which ultimately serves to widen participation in higher education.

We were particularly glad to see the firm commitment to the idea that contextual admissions should be designed, implemented, and evaluated as a ‘widening access initiative’ (p.6) rather than a recruitment tool. The guide is explicit that:

Contextual admissions exist as a widening participation intervention to take account of structural inequality, not to drive recruitment. Contextual offers must never be used to secure acceptances or influence applicant decision-making.

(p.4)

We agree that some contextual consideration of university applications is necessary, given the various social and educational inequalities that impact applicants’ attainment and prior experiences. Not to do this would mean that admissions processes mistake privilege for merit and ‘judg[e] [applicants] based on barriers beyond their control’ (p.3).

Within HERE@Manchester, this new guidance prompted several questions and reflections. We share two of these questions below, with the aim of contributing to a constructive debate on the future of contextual admissions in English higher education.

Does the sector currently practice contextual admissions for widening participation? If not, how far does practice deviate from this principle?

As mentioned, the guidance is clear that contextual admissions should be considered a ‘widening access initiative’ (p.6) rather than a recruitment tool. However, the guidance does not indicate the extent to which this reflects current practice, nor whether this requires a substantial shift in approach for many universities.

We (as a sector) don’t actually know how contextual admissions policies are developed and enacted. It is likely that admissions teams in different universities will work differently with widening participation professionals, and that the design, implementation and evaluation of such policies will involve a range of compromises between these stakeholders. There is therefore a need for in-depth research to explore these compromises, and the extent to which these local policies align with the principles in UUK’s guidance.

We also believe there is an opportunity to further clarify what appropriate and inappropriate practice would look like. There may well be a range of situations in which widening participation goals align with recruitment appropriately.

Our stance is that contextual admissions can be considered a widening participation intervention when designed and implemented to address the impact of structural barriers in university admissions. This chimes with UUK’s guidance, and the talk of universities drawing upon ‘the latest research and evidence’ (p.11), using ‘valid measures of structural disadvantage’ (p.11), and articulating these as a ‘theory of change to establish what their contextual interventions are intended to achieve’ (p.12). These should be described and evaluated along with other widening participation activities in Access and Participation Plans.

In contrast, it would be inappropriate to design and implement contextual admissions policies to increase the number of firm offer holders at a given university. If this is the primary driver of the policy, or if these recruitment concerns are used to decide the nature of the policy (say the size of the grade-reduction in contextual offers), then this shifts the policy into a recruitment tool, which we would consider inappropriate.

We believe it is questionable how many contextual admissions policies would be considered widening participation interventions under the definitions above. For this reason, we believe there is particular value in providing further guidance in this area.

What’s the route forward? How can we move to a system where contextual admissions does more to contribute to widening participation?

Although the guidance does not tackle this question head-on, there appears to be an implicit assumption that contextual admissions can be reformed to better contribute to widening participation goals through the action of individual universities. In other words, it is through the action of individual universities, say, in adopting evidence-based design and evaluation of their policies, that contextual admissions can shift to best support widening participation.

We see two potential issues with this approach.

First, evaluating the impact of contextual admissions on widening participation is far from a simple and technical task. Let’s explain this through an example.

A university evaluates its contextual admissions policy and finds that students who entered their institution with a two-grade reduction were slightly more likely to drop out in their first year, compared with their peers, and that they demonstrated slightly lower attainment during university.

There are multiple competing explanations of the gaps. This could be driven by:

Students enter higher education with less potential to succeed than their peers.

Students face the same structural barriers during their time in higher education.

The university has limited support and pedagogical practice to support these students upon entering higher education.

A simple evaluation, especially one that draws on quantitative administrative data, is unlikely to be able to judge the relative merit of each explanation. Moreover, the evaluation would not be able to directly answer the question: how much of a gap in retention or success is acceptable? This isn’t a purely technical question, but one that depends on the weight we give to the values of diversity and inclusion. Evaluation in this area is necessarily complex, with gaps in retention and success not necessarily evidencing the need to reform and restrict contextual admissions policies. (We look forward to engaging with Prof Anna Zimdars and TASO who are working within this broad area.)

A second potential issue with this route to change relates to wider structural forces.

The English higher education system has placed providers into competition with one another for students. This competition has intensified over time, particularly with the shift to uncapped entry and the reduction in the unit of resource per student. In such a climate, universities are working in a system that incentivises them to prioritise strategies for student recruitment. These incentives serve to penalise institutions that do not utilise levers to drive recruitment; universities that do not use contextual admissions to prioritise recruitment goals lose out on funding compared with their competitors.

For this reason, we would question whether contextual admissions can contribute further to widening participation without additional forms of centralisation.

There are elements of centralisation contained within the guidance. For example, there is discussion of taking a more consistent approach, both in terms of a central repository for contextual admissions policies and the use of shared language (p.15). Similarly, the guidance takes a strong stance on the appropriateness of different metrics, with area-based indicators labelled ‘contextually useful but not to be used in isolation’ (p.9). This implies there may be opportunities for greater consistency, based on this centralised approach to assess indicator validity.

Our question is whether the best route to embed this consistency is through the action of individual universities. Specifically, does it make sense for individual universities to be responsible for evaluating the evidence of a structural barrier, especially when they are subject to the market pressures noted above, rather than this being accounted for in a more centralised way?

There are plenty of international examples of more centralised ways of approaching contextualisation. In Australia, the ATAR (Australian Tertiary Admissions Rank) students can apply for adjustment at state-level to contextualise their result, based on personal characteristics, indigenous status or prior educational circumstances. Closer to home, Scottish universities have taken a centralised approach towards the language around contextual admissions, with each university providing ‘minimum entry requirements’, making the application process clearer for students.

In summary, our research group welcomes UUK’s recent publication Contextual Admission: A guide to fair and transparent practice as an important intervention. In this piece, we hope to contribute to the debate – both in reflecting on the size and nature of any changes in approach, as well as in thinking through the routes to enable contextual admissions to further contribute to widening participation.

title: In an age of climate disaster, more states offer students a way to show they are ‘climate literate’

The post In an age of climate disaster, more states offer students a way to show they are ‘climate literate’ appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
As a student at a high school not far from Denver’s main airport, Anthony Muñoz wondered whether the jet fuel from airplanes flying above his campus was harming living things.

An avid gardener, Muñoz partnered with a local university to create a garden on the campus of his charter school, Vista Academy, filling it with native plants that could detect ground-level ozone pollution. He also worked with climate scientists from the National Center for Atmospheric Research, a federal office in nearby Boulder, who directed Muñoz on what data to collect, what the condition of leaves reveals about air quality and why milkweed matters for monarch butterfly migration.

“One garden’s a very good data source,” said Muñoz. “Colorado’s so beautiful, and I would hate to see it wilt away.”

Muñoz built the “ozone garden” for his capstone project as part of Colorado’s seal of climate literacy, a statewide initiative that pairs climate-focused coursework with hands-on community service. To earn the seal — an endorsement on high school diplomas and transcripts — students must complete at least two advanced courses that cover the Earth’s climate systems and an approved project that tackles a climate issue in their community.

Since 2024, when Colorado lawmakers approved the seal, 26 of the state’s 179 school districts have adopted it, according to Lyra Colorado, an education nonprofit that advocates for the seal. Now, the model is spreading to other states. Maine adopted its own climate seal earlier this year, and California just signed into law a bill to establish the seal for graduates there. Youth coalitions have pushed for the policy in Hawaii and Minnesota, with varying success.

Proponents of the seal argue that young people must understand and combat climate change, without waiting for political leaders to reach consensus on how it should be taught in schools. They also hope the endorsement will connect students to a rapidly expanding green workforce, preparing them to work on solar grids and climate-resilient farms or in water resource management and urban heat mitigation. And, as climate change begins to alter almost every aspect of human life, the seal could offer anxious teenagers a sense of agency and ability to make some difference.

“Where we can make the most difference is often in our local community,” said Laura Schifter, a senior fellow with the Aspen Institute’s This is Planet Ed, a climate education group. She said the seal offers students a chance to learn about climate change, a topic rarely covered in depth in K-12 classrooms, and called it “a really promising policy.”

Still, the seal has faced hurdles, including tight school district budgets, concern about new burdens on schools and the federal government’s attempts to refute climate science.

Lance Izumi, senior director of education studies with the free market think tank Pacific Research Institute in California, which has been criticized in the past for sharing disinformation about climate change, said he’d rather see students focusing on the fundamentals of science rather than what he considers activist community projects. He noted only a third of students in the Golden State test as proficient in science.

“Diverting focus away from foundational science learning could worsen California’s already abysmal performance levels,” he wrote in an email.

Related: Interested in climate change and education? Sign up for our newsletter.

The idea for the seal originated with Lyra Colorado, the nonprofit in Denver that supports community-based education programs. Rural students and educators the group was working with on another climate-related project said they wanted a way to explore climate change as a reality in their daily lives, not just through a dense unit in a textbook, according to Mary Seawell, Lyra’s CEO.

To earn the seal, students need to complete two classes that promote “climate literacy,” or basic principles of climate change such as its causes and how to mitigate it. One of them must be a science class, such as environmental studies, biology or earth science. The other course can be in any discipline, including the humanities or fine arts. For example, this year Denver Public Schools will build lessons about climate change into its state-mandated civics course, Seawell said. Students also must complete a school-approved capstone project in their local community; a running list of student projects includes ones related to beaver dams, building trails, snow science and forestry management.

The program is voluntary; districts can choose whether to offer the seal on diplomas, and individual students in those districts can decide to pursue it or not. An estimated 1,200 students have received it so far, said Seawell.

Funding, though, has been a challenge: State lawmakers provided less than $20,000 for the seal’s rollout. Many students fund their projects out of pocket or, like Muñoz, secure grants. He cowrote a $1 million grant proposal to the city to pay for the gardens at his school. Lyra created its own grant program to help local schools pay for teachers’ time, student projects and even graduation cords.

Muñoz, now a sophomore studying mechanical engineering at the Colorado School of Mines, said the seal allowed him to learn climate leadership skills. He’s now vice president of the college’s environmental club and tries to inspire his peers to take action.

“Are you going to think beyond yourself and help not only those in need but the environment, or will you sit back and wait for someone else to change the world for you?” he said.

As more students like Muñoz graduate with the seal, many have started to work on climate issues at their colleges and in new states.

Rylan Neumann graduated last year from the Boulder Valley School District, enrolling that fall at the University of California, Berkeley, to study environmental economics. Almost immediately, she joined an eco-club and boarded a train to Sacramento, where she lobbied state lawmakers in support of the state’s pending climate seal bill.

“Getting more students involved in climate action and how they’ll be impacted in the future is essential,” she said. “Students are the future. We’re the ones growing up in this world.”

Young people have pushed for the seal in other states too. In Hawaii, a student member of the state board of education championed the endorsement for high schools on the islands. The Minnesota Youth Council, a state advisory board with representatives from middle and high schools, recommended the seal during this year’s legislative session.

Related: Education that convinces kids the world isn’t doomed

State education officials in Maine, meanwhile, adopted the seal directly to avoid legislative debate.

“Students want to be involved in climate action, in environmental literacy, in green careers,” said Teddy Lyman, the K-12 climate education specialist in Maine. “They’re often doing the work already but don’t have the recognition. They didn’t see a sort of pathway to continue that work and embark on that as a potential career.”

Maine already offers a seal of biliteracy, which recognizes students for proficiency in two or more languages. That made it easier to adopt the new seal, Lyman said.

The seal also complements existing state guidelines that require schools to incorporate traditional ecological knowledge, or Indigenous studies, into all classes, said Lyman. He added that grounding the seal in local capstone projects also could lower climate distress among youth.

“No more global doom and gloom,” Lyman said. “Students can feel empowered to make a difference in their community. They’re not trying to solve something for the U.N. They’re advocating at their town committee instead.”

During a spring pilot across nine high schools, Lyman expected roughly a dozen students to apply for the seal. Instead, he said, 57 seniors did.

Melissa Luetje teaches science at Freeport High School, which enrolls about 600 students, many of whom earn money on lobster boats and aquaculture farms growing oysters or seaweed. Warming and rising sea levels have hit nearby Casco Bay hard, eroding coastal infrastructure and flooding surface streets.

The Gulf of Maine is warming faster than almost any other body of water on the planet, Luetje said. “That means all eyes are on us. There’s so much good science happening in our backyard.”

For a seal-approved class she teaches on research, students will monitor woodlands for insect damage, develop new ways to compost or commodify an invasive crab species, and work on a sustainable fishery.

“How climate impacts the coastal community is very different from the interior or a city,” Luetje said. “It’s up to each community to figure out what they value and how they want to roll this out.”

Related: The greening of career education: Students learn new skills they’ll need as climate change advances

As the seal expands, proponents have tried to connect the high school endorsement directly to career and technical education and green workforce pipelines.

Lyra Colorado has started working with higher education institutions like Colorado Mountain College to align the seal with certification in the skilled trades, such as heat pump installation, solar grid maintenance or sustainable agriculture. She hopes universities will offer a partial minor or a course credit for incoming first-year students who have the climate endorsement.

At the same time, President Donald Trump has attacked climate change as a “hoax,” and new federal scrutiny of renewable energy projects threatens philanthropic support for such initiatives. The Treasury Department and Republicans in Congress have targeted the tax-exempt status of nonprofits that support climate causes, which Seawell said created a noticeable chilling effect among potential donors.

“Funders are worried,” she said.

The Trump administration has also tried to pull funding from and dismantle the National Center for Atmospheric Research, the climate research center that helped Muñoz with his school garden. He called the proposed cuts “devastating.”

Still, Muñoz, who plans to pursue biomedicine and one day become a professor, remains focused on climate issues.

He met virtually with students pushing for the seal in Minnesota. And he spent his first college break back at Vista Academy, assisting younger kids in the garden. They recently put the final touches on an elevated box designed for gardeners in wheelchairs.

And he’s writing code to make it easier for Vista students to continue collecting data in the ozone garden — even if it’s not clear when, or if, NCAR scientists will get to use the data.

Contact staff writer Neal Morton at 212-678-8247, on Signal at nealmorton.99, or via email at morton@hechingerreport.org.

title: Sliding student scores spark fresh calls to revisit how we're teaching math
summary: With recent high-profile assessments warning of sluggish and waning math skills among Canadian students, some experts say we need to revisit how we're teaching it, and to pay numeracy the same attention we've shown literacy in recent years.
full_text:
Earlier this week, Kendra Corbett stood at a blackboard breaking down an addition question for her Grade 3s, laying out step by step how to determine the answer and occasionally testing out suggestions her students called out.

A little later, she split her class into groups. Some youngsters played math games while others worked on an assignment using base ten blocks — manipulating the small plastic cubes, bars and squares (denoting units of one, 10 and 100, respectively). Corbett settled in with a handful of kids for a focused lesson on ordering numbers from least to greatest. All the activities allowed for practice learning three-digit numbers.

"We assume kids come in knowing what numbers actually mean. If they can count to 10, that doesn't necessarily mean they understand what 10 represents," said Corbett, a teacher in Upper Grand District School Board in Orangeville, Ont., some 60 kilometres northwest of Toronto.

"If they don't have the foundation of knowing what numbers actually mean and understanding of magnitude, then they're really going to struggle later on."

Knowledge and understanding of math rests on building blocks that students usually start developing in primary school. But with recent international and provincial assessments warning about sluggish and waning math skills among Canadian students — a slide that pre-dates the pandemic — some experts say we should revisit how we teach math and pay numeracy the same attention literacy has received in recent years.

What worries Canadian mathematician John Mighton are the changes happening over time, specifically the growth in students who are slipping to lower levels — where some can only handle basic math or are considered below functional numeracy — and the wider impact of that trend.

"That's a real threat to our country, to our economy, even to our political system. How can you think your way through problems that involve risk or probabilities or science if you can't do the simplest math?" said Mighton.

"It's a tragedy that we think math is not as important as it as and that we're not doing something about it."

Back in 2002, Mighton founded JUMP Math, an education charity that's grown to work with students and teachers in K-8 schools across Canada and abroad.

Teaching novices a new concept takes a different approach than teaching those already fluent in a topic, he says, yet much math instruction of the past 20 years has treated kids like experts before they're ready.

"From day one, you're given a lot of rich problems … highly contextualized, lots of complexity, lots of language. People don't feel they're really giving kids math unless they're doing that kind of problem," Mighton said.

"We mistake the end where we want to get kids to — we want them to be great chess players, great problem solvers — with the means to get them there," he said.

"Guide kids more, scaffold more, give more practice, build foundational knowledge, so the kids can become experts …When you do that, kids become much better problem-solvers."

Building a solid foundation and then strong reasoning and problem-solving skills are especially important amid the rise of artificial intelligence, he says.

"It's a dangerous idea that kids are just going to be able to deal with all the challenges that are coming from AI … if they don't have any domain-specific knowledge, particularly in mathematics.

"You're going to be so easily fooled and misled and you'll make disastrous decisions if you don't understand the math."

Not a return to rote learning

As with the recent shift toward more explicit, structured and phonics-led literacy teaching, there's a growing call for more systematic, teacher-led, direct instruction in math.

That doesn't mean rote learning, Mighton says, but does mean relying on evidence-based practices. He encourages teachers to use screenings, for instance, and regular low-stakes assessments to help them to make adjustments that propel students' progression.

There's a wealth of research about how children learn — on their attention spans, their ability to absorb information, barriers to that, and more — yet that research doesn't always translate into classrooms nor into the training that aspiring and working teachers receive, says neuroscientist Daniel Ansari, a professor of psychology and education at Western University in London, Ont.

He also advocates breaking up math learning into multiple, simplified steps, because it helps developing minds more readily pick up information.

"Sometimes teaching can assume that children start out as experts and they are required immediately to focus on their understanding, explaining their answers. And these sorts of things can overwhelm their cognitive systems and thereby prevent information making its way into long-term memory," he said.

Ansari says educators can absolutely strike a "balance between explicit instruction and letting children discover things working by themselves," but adds teachers must keep in mind what's developmentally appropriate and what learners are ready for.

Take timed practice — a.k.a. those "mad minute" sheets with rows of addition, subtraction, multiplication or division questions to be answered as quickly as possible — as an example.

Introduced too early, it overwhelms cognitive capacity, Ansari says. But once students have some time to learn and a bit of practice, "mad minutes serve as a way of increasing and deepening their fluency — and then it can also become something really fun."

Rather than touting a "back to basics" mentality, Ansari instead suggests we consider "how can we improve things further, pick some things that we maybe discarded too early? Keep some things we're doing right now, but reassess some others."

Back in Orangeville, Upper Grand K-12 math lead Ashley Kozak has overseen a multi-pronged plan to improve early math learning. It includes central math facilitators, creating new teaching resources, employing an early math screener and, for the schools with the greatest need, sending in support teachers to deliver focused tutoring.

Updated math training for Grade 1 and Grade 3 teachers and principals has also boosted educator confidence, Kozak says, adding the board saw improvement in its latest EQAO results.

While she loves seeing kids' "a-ha" moments when visiting math classes, she says it's even better seeing students confidently approach the next questions.

"It's more than memorization. It's about problem-solving. It's about making those connections," she said. "Seeing that ... makes me feel like 'OK, we got this. We can do it.'"

title: Meet Wileidy Feliciano-Rivera, seventh-grader whose plantain mulch cut weeds 53%
summary: Wileidy Feliciano-Rivera, a seventh-grader from Puerto Rico, transformed discarded plantain peels into biodegradable mulch. This innovative project addressed plastic waste and showcased potential agricultural benefits. EcoMusa, the resultant mulch, effectively reduced weed growth during testing while retaining moisture and lowering soil temperatures. Wileidy's work has garnered recognition as a finalist in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge.
full_text:
Wileidy Feliciano-Rivera, the Puerto Rico seventh-grader who turned discarded school-cafeteria plantain peels into biodegradable farm mulch (Image Credit: Society for Science)

A Puerto Rico seventh-grader has found an unusual use for something that would normally be thrown away after lunch: plantain peels. Wileidy Feliciano-Rivera collected discarded peels from her school cafeteria and turned them into a biodegradable mulch designed to control weeds in agricultural soil. In four-week tests, her two plantain-based mulch versions reduced weed growth by 47% and 53% compared with uncovered soil, while also helping retain moisture and lower soil temperatures. Her project has now earned her a place among the 30 finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge, according to the Society for Science, the competition organiser.

From cafeteria waste to an agricultural material

Wileidy, a seventh-grade student at Escuela Intermedia Rafael Irizarry Rivera in Peñuelas, Puerto Rico, began the project by looking at two problems connected to agriculture: plastic waste and the disposal of organic material. Plastic mulch is used by farmers to cover soil, suppress weeds and help retain moisture. But after use, plastic mulch can become agricultural waste. Wileidy explored whether a biodegradable material could perform some of the same functions without relying on conventional plastic. Her attention turned to plantain peels being discarded at her school. Instead of treating them as waste, she investigated whether they could serve as the raw material for a bioplastic mulch. The resulting project was called EcoMusa. Its name reflects the use of Musa paradisiaca, the scientific name used in the project for the plantain source material.

How Wileidy made EcoMusa

The young researcher processed the discarded plantain peels and used them to produce sheets of bioplastic. According to Society for Science, she first chopped the peels into smaller pieces before blending them with water, acetic acid, glycerin and cornstarch. The mixture was then heated and poured into trays, where it was allowed to dry and form sheets. Wileidy produced two versions of the material, known as EcoMusa 1 and EcoMusa 2. She then tested whether they could work as mulch by placing them over soil and comparing their performance with uncovered soil and commercial black plastic mulch. The experiment was designed to look at more than just whether weeds appeared. Wileidy also monitored soil moisture, soil temperature and how the plant-based material degraded during the test period.

Weed growth dropped by up to 53%

The experiment ran for four weeks, during which Wileidy tracked weed density in the different test areas. EcoMusa 1 reduced weed growth by 47%, while EcoMusa 2 produced a 53% reduction compared with uncovered soil. The Society for Science reported that the two versions performed comparably to the commercial black plastic mulch used in the experiment. The mulch also affected conditions beneath the soil covering. The plantain-based materials kept soil temperatures between one and three degrees Celsius lower than uncovered soil and helped retain moisture. Those results suggest that the material could perform some of the functions expected from agricultural mulch. However, the experiment was limited to four weeks, so the findings do not establish how the material would perform over a full growing season or across different crops and farming conditions.

A project linking food and plastic waste

EcoMusa brings together two types of waste that are often treated separately. The plantain peels used in Wileidy's experiment were food waste from her school cafeteria. Turning them into a bioplastic mulch gave that discarded material another potential use. At the same time, the project explores an alternative to conventional plastic mulch. Because EcoMusa is biodegradable, its intended purpose is not simply to replace one form of plastic with another, but to create a material that can break down after use. The project therefore goes beyond the idea of simply making a new material. It examines whether a readily available waste product can be converted into something useful for agriculture.

A place among 2026's young science finalists

Wileidy's research has now taken her beyond her school laboratory. Her EcoMusa project was selected among the 30 finalists for the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. The competition, run by the Society for Science, recognises middle-school students conducting research in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. The finalists are scheduled to participate in Finals Week in Washington, DC, from October 23 to 28, with more than $100,000 in prizes available. For Wileidy, the project began with a simple observation about material being discarded at school. She turned those peels into a research question and then tested whether the resulting material could do a useful job in agriculture.

What the experiment shows

EcoMusa is not yet evidence that plantain-peel mulch can replace commercial agricultural plastic on a large scale. More research would be needed to determine its durability, degradation rate, performance across different environments and suitability for different crops. But Wileidy's four-week experiment produced measurable results. Her two mulch versions reduced weed growth by up to 53%, while also helping retain soil moisture and moderate soil temperature. The project demonstrates how an everyday waste product can become the starting point for a scientific experiment. What began as discarded plantain peels from a Puerto Rico school cafeteria has become a biodegradable agricultural material that Wileidy is now testing as a possible way to manage weeds while addressing waste.

End of Article

title: Porti turistici, giro d’affari previsto in crescita nel 2027
summary: Per gli ormeggi i dati positivi di quest’anno, proseguiranno anche il prossimo. Perocchio (Assomarinas): «Buone prospettive per un quinquennio»
full_text:
Buone prospettive si profilano per la portualità turistica italiana, sia per il 2027, sia, prevede il presidente di Assomarinas, Roberto Perocchio, «per il prossimo quinquennio». L’associazione confindustriale che raggruppa le marine dedicate al diporto ha appena compilato l’indagine 2026 sul settore, che comprende le previsioni relative all’anno prossimo e che Il Sole 24 Ore è in grado di anticipare.

Per quanto riguarda l’andamento 2026 degli ormeggi stanziali, il giro d’affari segna +2,96% sul 2025, con un positivo andamento del mercato dei superyacht, si legge nello studio, che incrementano la loro presenza sulle coste italiane. Per il 2027 si attende un ulteriore +1,36%: una stabilizzazione della richiesta di ormeggi stanziali, a causa del calo di vendite di imbarcazioni nuove. Per quanto riguarda gli ormeggi in transito, il 2026 ha segnato +4,36%, con un assestamento, rileva Assomarinas, nelle imbarcazioni di dimensioni piccole e medie, ma un incremento di unità di maggiori dimensioni che consente la crescita complessiva del fatturato di quel servizio. Le previsioni per il 2027 segnano addirittura un +7,43%, connesso soprattutto al charter di barche e ai superyacht internazionali.

Marine al lavoro per creare nuovi posti barca

Quest’anno, spiega Perocchio, «il volume d’affari è ancora cresciuto, quasi fino al 3%, per gli ormeggi stanziali, che sono il core per la maggior parte dei porti turistici». La crescita meno spiccata prefigurata per il 2027 è dovuta, afferma, al fatto che «siamo arrivati a livelli di saturazione dei porti esistenti e che molto di più non si riesce a fare. Del resto, è già iniziata la marcia verso la realizzazione di nuove strutture (sono circa 20mila i posti barca in programmazione nei prossimi 10 anni, ndr).
